analysis: Twenty-eight pieces of Chinese export blue and white with gilt, catalogued as 19th century. The photographs argue earlier: a drum-form teapot with domed lid and gilt finial, a matching covered sugar, handleless tea bowls AND handled coffee cans in the same service, and a spearhead-and-cell border of a type that belongs to c.1790-1820 rather than late Qing. The close-up of a saucer shows hand-painted underglaze cobalt with visible brush modulation -- not transfer -- and a gilt rim worn from use rather than fresh. A complete matched export tea service of this date and this many pieces is a $1,200-2,500 lot; the teapot alone is $300-500. At $500-700 the house has catalogued it as generic export china and priced it by the piece. Best straight value in the ceramics.
problems: Twenty-eight pieces means twenty-eight chances for a chip, a hairline or a stained crack, and the group shot cannot rule any of that out -- lift each saucer at preview and check foot rims and cup handles. Gilt is already worn in places; that is honest age, not damage, but it is where the piece looks tired. Two dish forms appear to be replacements from a near-matching service, which is normal in a survivor of this size but should be counted. Nothing here is marked, so the date rests on form and border, not a stamp.
patience: Moderate. Export tea wares surface constantly at Thomaston, but complete services of this date and count do not -- most of what comes through is late-19th-c. Canton in ones and twos.

analysis: A four-gallon F.B. Norton & Co., Worcester, Massachusetts salt-glazed stoneware jug with a large slip-trailed cobalt floral spray. The impressed maker's mark and the '4' capacity are both crisp and legible in the photograph, which settles the attribution without preview. F.B. Norton & Co. ran in Worcester roughly 1865-1885, so this clears the 1926 line comfortably and carries a documented American maker -- two of the five criteria at once. The decoration is generous and well drawn: a full three-element spray running most of the height of the shoulder, not the token clover you get on the cheap end. Body is clean grey with good salt orange-peel, the handle is intact, and the base shows honest wear.
problems: Decorated Norton jugs are faked, but faking a four-gallon jug is not economic and the mark here has the slightly under-inked, uneven strike of a real impressed stamp rather than the too-even look of a modern die. Check the interior for a through-crack -- big jugs commonly have a spider off the base that does not show from outside -- and run a fingernail round the lip for chips under the glaze. Cobalt has bled slightly in firing, which is period-correct.
patience: Moderate. New England decorated stoneware runs at Thomaston regularly, but a legible Worcester mark with a full floral at this size is the better half of that supply.

analysis: A two-gallon Wm. E. Warner, West Troy, New York stoneware jug with a simple three-leaf cobalt clover and what appears to be the original turned wooden bung still in the mouth. Warner worked West Troy in the 1850s-60s; genuinely antique, genuinely a named pottery. But the decoration is the plainest grade -- three brushed leaves, no stem work, no bird, no flourish -- and decoration is what carries value in American stoneware. The surviving stopper is a nice small piece of completeness that most of these have lost.
problems: There is a rust-brown stain running down the left shoulder, which reads as an iron inclusion or a long-standing surface stain rather than a crack, but confirm. Faint diagonal scratches across the lower body. The mark is only partly legible in the photograph. Plain jugs are the most common thing in the category and the market for them is soft.
patience: High. Undecorated and lightly decorated New York stoneware jugs come through in quantity; there is no reason to reach.

analysis: James Hamilton & Co. of Greensboro, Pennsylvania -- a well-documented western Pennsylvania stoneware operation, and a marked crock is a marked crock. Estimated $100-200, which is where plain Hamilton crocks actually trade. The lowest-priced lot in the ceramics and one of the few where the estimate is not doing any work.
problems: Only two photographs and no interior shot. Crocks are the most utilitarian survivors in the category, so expect rim chips, a scratched interior and possibly a stabilised freeze crack. Pennsylvania rather than New England, which costs it regional interest with a Maine buyer.
patience: High. Marked crocks are the entry level of the stoneware market and are always available.

analysis: A large hand-painted porcelain charger, portrait of a young woman in a plumed bonnet, signed H. Catelin lower right, on a Boulenger & Cie, Montereau blank. This is the real thing and the photograph shows it: the face is properly modelled with wet-blended flesh tones, the feathers are built up in successive fired layers, and the ground is a printed-and-gilt blue floral diaper that has the slightly irregular gilt of hand finishing. Late-19th-century French decorated porcelain by a legible hand, comfortably pre-1926, on a documented factory body. At $300-500 estimate this is one of the few decorative ceramics in the sale where the price and the quality line up.
problems: H. Catelin is a decorator's signature, not a name with an auction record -- per the standing principle, do not pay named-maker money for a signature nobody has indexed. The value is in the painting, not the name. Some scattered loss to the gilt trellis in the lower left of the bodice area. Verify it is a plaque or charger rather than a plate with a fitted hanger, and check the reverse for a repaired hanging hole.
patience: Moderate. Painted French chargers of this quality run through regional sales a few times a year; ones with a legible signature and a factory mark are the smaller share.

analysis: Catalogued as a 'Lille 1737' faience platter. It is not a 1737 platter. 'Lille 1737' is a retro-mark used by late-19th-century French faience decorators, and everything visible here says c.1875-1900: an oval scallop-edged platter, a tavern scene inscribed D'APRES TENIERS -- after Teniers, which by the standing principle means copy -- signed H. Clerc (the catalogue reads it as M. Clerc), and a rim of ribbon-tied rose and forget-me-not swags in the sweet Boulenger-Montereau manner. Note that lot 1153 is a Boulenger & Cie, Montereau plaque by another hand; these two are almost certainly the same consignment. Still a genuine antique, still hand-painted, but the date on the mark is decoration.
problems: The 1737 date in the title is the trap: anyone bidding on it as an 18th-century piece is paying four times what it is. Crazing throughout the glaze. It is displayed on a wire plate hanger whose arms are visible over the rim -- check what the wire has done to the glaze at the contact points. 'After Teniers' means this is a copy of a copy: a 19th-c. faience painter working from an engraving after a 17th-c. painting.
patience: High. Late-19th-c. French decorated faience is deep supply and mostly sells below estimate.

analysis: Three early Massachusetts porcelain-enamel automobile plates: two of the 'MASS. AUTOMOBILE REGISTER' type (numbers 12478 and 6042, c.1904-07) and one dated 1909 with the low three-digit number 978. All are genuine period vitreous enamel on steel with the correct cobalt ground and white numerals -- the enamel loss shows base steel and old rust underneath rather than a modern repaint. Comfortably pre-1926 and catalogued to the year on the dated example. Low numbers are what the automobilia market pays for, and 978 is very low. Estimated $300-400 for three.
problems: All three have enamel chipping -- the 12478 plate has significant loss along the lower centre and around the slots, the 6042 has losses at the top edge. Condition is what separates a $150 early plate from a $500 one, and these are mid-grade. Grouped as three, so you cannot cherry-pick the 1909. Automobilia is a collector market with no overlap with the rest of this collection.
patience: Moderate. Early porcelain plates surface steadily, but pre-1910 Massachusetts examples with low numbers are the desirable end.

analysis: Rolls-Royce Phantom I handbook, registration and license plate as a three-piece paper-and-metal group at $600-800. Phantom I ran 1925-1931, so the material straddles the antique line rather than clearing it. This is Rolls-Royce marque ephemera, which sells to Rolls collectors and nobody else; there is no overlap with a Maine antiques collection and no criteria fit.
problems: Estimate sits at the top of the band for what is, in collecting terms, paperwork. Paper condition cannot be assessed from a group photograph. Value depends almost entirely on whether the documents tie to a surviving chassis number.
patience: High. Marque ephemera is a specialist trade with regular supply.

analysis: A Massachusetts license plate with its 1966 RMV mailing envelope, estimated $100-200. Sixty years old, so it misses the antique line by four decades, and 1960s plates are common. The envelope is the interesting part -- unopened original mailers are a small niche -- but not a $100-200 part.
problems: Estimate is roughly double the market. Nothing here fits any of the five criteria.

analysis: Twelve Minton service plates at $300-500. Minton is a documented maker, but gilt-rim service plates are the definition of dinnerware in quantity -- a category the standing brief already flags as a weak market, and one that has kept getting weaker as formal dining collapsed. Twelve plates at $25-40 each is what these actually make, and that is before the buyer's premium.
problems: Estimate is at or above the retail market, let alone the auction market. No date given, and Minton service plates span 1890-1960 with no visual break. Storage and shelf space costs more than the plates are worth.
patience: Very high. There is a Minton service plate lot in most sales.

analysis: Twenty-nine Minton gilt-rim plates at $300-500 -- the same proposition as 1041 with more shelf space. At $10-17 a plate the estimate is not outrageous, but the total is a commitment to storing twenty-nine plates for a market that is not coming back.
problems: Quantity dinnerware, weak market, no date. Twenty-nine pieces means a near certainty of chips and knife scoring; assume some are unusable.

analysis: Twelve Minton dinner service plates retailed by Tiffany & Co., $500-700. The Tiffany retailer's mark adds something -- it certifies a first-quality blank and pulls a second collector base -- but not enough to lift a quantity dinnerware lot into this collection. Twelve gilt service plates are $30-45 each on a good day.
problems: Estimate is above the market even with the Tiffany mark doing work. No date. Same storage and condition exposure as the other service-plate lots.

analysis: A twenty-piece Meissen 'Indian Flowers' (Indianische Blumen) dessert set at $600-800. Meissen is the one porcelain name where the mark carries real, liquid value, and Indianische Blumen is an 18th-century pattern still in production -- which is exactly the problem for dating. At $30-40 a piece the estimate is below what Meissen retails at and about what it makes at auction, so this is the one quantity-china lot in the sale where the maker's name genuinely floors the price.
problems: The crossed-swords mark has to be read carefully: the number and configuration of cancellation strokes, dots and the pommel shape date the piece and separate first quality from seconds and outlet ware. Post-1926 Meissen is common and this could easily be 1950s. No date given, hence 'border'. Twenty pieces of dessert china is still twenty pieces of dessert china.
patience: Moderate. Meissen groups surface a few times a year; a matched twenty-piece set less often.

analysis: Ten Wedgwood transferware plates from the Bowdoin College series. Genuinely interesting to a midcoast Maine buyer -- Bowdoin is in Brunswick, twenty minutes from Bath, and hyper-local material sells to a small committed audience. But the Wedgwood American college series began in 1927 and ran for decades, so despite the antique look these are almost certainly post-1926 and fail the age criterion on a technicality that happens to be true. Ten plates for $200-300 is $20-30 each; the college series trades at $15-30.
problems: Estimate is at the top of the market. Wedgwood college plates are not scarce -- Bowdoin, Bates, Colby and Harvard sets turn up in Maine sales constantly. Buy this for the Brunswick views on a wall, not as an antique.
patience: Very high. This is the most reliably available Maine-institutional ceramic there is.

analysis: A Roseville 'Rosecraft Hexagon' double bud vase in the green matte, the gate form with a moulded medallion and a raised ivory blossom on the bridge. The photograph reads as genuine: the moulding is crisp at the hexagon corners and the medallion, the matte glaze breaks tonally across the ridges rather than sitting flat and uniform, and the ivory slip decoration has the slight bleed of a period application. Rosecraft Hexagon dates c.1924-25, which puts it right on the 1926 line -- 'border', not 'antique'. Good Arts and Crafts form and the most attractive Roseville shape in this sale.
problems: The estimate is the trap the brief already names. Roseville corrected hard and has not recovered; Rosecraft Hexagon gate vases sell $175-350, not $400-600. Check the base for a hairline running up from the foot -- the gate form is structurally weak at the bridge joins -- and check the bridge cut-out for a restored break, which is the standard damage on this shape and is easy to miss under matte glaze.
patience: Moderate to high. Roseville is everywhere, though Rosecraft is a less common line than Pine Cone or Magnolia.

analysis: Four studio pottery vessels including Andrew Hill and Eugene Deutsch, $300-500. This is the first of a nine-lot studio-pottery consignment running 1135-1151 -- Sequoia Miller, Aldermaston, Richard G. Robertson, American Paradox, Deutsch, Hill. Identify the block and treat it as one decision rather than nine. All of it is post-war, none of it approaches 1926, and none of it hits any of the five criteria. Eugene Deutsch (Chicago, 1907-1980) is mildly collected and is the only name here with a market.
problems: Whole consignment is estimated at gallery levels rather than auction levels. Studio pottery is the most consignor-optimistic category in any sale.

analysis: Two American Paradox Pottery pit-fired studio vessels at $400-600. Pit-fired contemporary studio ware with no date, no established secondary market and a maker name that does not index. Part of the 1135-1151 studio block.
problems: Estimate is roughly three times any plausible resale. Pit-fired surfaces are fragile and mark easily. Nothing about this is antique, precious, Nouveau, documented or Maine.

analysis: Two Richard G. Robertson (American, 1943-2016) Bizen-style stoneware pieces, $300-500. Dated by artist lifespan, so squarely modern. 'Bizen-style' is the cataloguer declining to commit to anything -- it is an American potter working in a Japanese idiom, not Bizen ware. Part of the 1135-1151 studio block.
problems: Robertson has almost no auction record. Estimate is a gallery number.

analysis: Sequoia Miller studio pottery teapot, $250-350. Miller is a living American potter, catalogued as contemporary -- one of four of his pieces in this consignment (1141, 1143, 1145, 1149). Living-artist studio pottery bought at auction almost always resells below what the same piece costs from the maker, and four of them in one sale guarantees they compete with each other.
problems: Four lots by one living potter in one sale is oversupply of a market that barely exists at auction. Estimate is at or above studio retail.
patience: Very high -- there are three more in this sale alone.

analysis: Sequoia Miller studio pottery jar, $300-400. See 1141 -- second of four Miller lots, same reasoning. Contemporary, no criteria fit, estimate at retail.
problems: Oversupplied within the sale itself.

analysis: Sequoia Miller studio pottery vase, $400-600 -- the highest-estimated of the four Miller lots and the same objection. A living potter's work at auction is priced against his own current studio prices, and the auction number here exceeds them.
problems: Highest estimate in the Miller group with nothing to justify the step up over 1141 or 1143.

analysis: Sequoia Miller studio pottery pitcher, $300-400. Fourth Miller lot. Same call.
problems: Same as 1141.

analysis: Three English Aldermaston Pottery articles at $300-500. Aldermaston was Alan Caiger-Smith's pottery, founded 1955, and his tin-glaze lustreware is genuinely collected -- in Britain. In an American regional sale it is an unrecognised name and sells accordingly. Post-war, so no age criterion.
problems: The UK market for Caiger-Smith does not travel; American auction results run well below British ones. Three unspecified 'articles' with no dimensions or forms named.

analysis: 'Possibly English Aldermaston' large glazed dish, $250-350. 'Possibly' is the cataloguer with an unmarked piece and a hunch -- price it as the anonymous studio dish it is, which is $80-200. Part of the 1135-1151 block.
problems: Attribution is explicitly a guess in the title itself. Even if right, see 1147.

analysis: A large copper milk jug with spout, $200-300. Decorative copper and brass is one of the categories the standing brief names as a weak market, and it has not moved. Undated, unmarked, and French or English farm copper of this type has been imported by the container for fifty years -- much of it made for the decorator trade rather than for milk.
problems: No date, no mark, no maker. Modern reproduction dairy copper is indistinguishable in a photograph; the tells are machine-rolled seams and even wall thickness, both of which need the piece in hand. Estimate is double the market.

analysis: Three porcelain-knob walking canes, and the photograph shows all three are period: a cobalt-and-gilt Sevres-manner knob on an ebonised shaft with a collar stamped STERLING; a yellow-ground knob over a long porcelain-and-gilt-brass ferrule section with a hand-painted portrait cartouche, on malacca; and a green-trellis-and-rose knob with a cast gilt-metal collar on a bamboo shaft. All read c.1880-1900 and all are genuinely antique. Individually each is a $150-300 cane. Grouped at $600-800 the estimate takes the whole retail spread up front.
problems: 'STERLING' on a cane collar is a mount, not metal content -- the standing rule about silver-mounted objects applies and there is no melt floor here worth calculating. Canes take damage at the joint between knob and shaft; check each for a regluing and for hairlines in the porcelain, particularly the portrait ferrule, which is the most vulnerable and the most valuable element. Three-item group means you cannot take just the portrait cane.
patience: Moderate. Cane groups run through Thomaston a few times a year but porcelain-knob examples with hand-painted panels are the smaller share.

analysis: An inlaid mahogany tea caddy with its mixing bowl. The mixing bowl is the point: most Georgian caddies lost their central cut-glass bowl within a generation, and a surviving original roughly doubles the piece. If the inlay and the carcase are period c.1800-1830 this is a genuine antique object with a real use-history. Estimated $600-800.
problems: Caddies are among the most convincingly faked Georgian small furniture -- Edwardian and 1920s revival caddies use the same woods and stringing, and modern Indian-made 'Georgian' caddies are everywhere. Judge it on the interior: period caddies show oxidised, unfinished secondary wood, hand-cut dovetails at the corners, and lead-lined or foil-lined compartments with genuine tea staining. Confirm the mixing bowl is original to the caddy and not a later cut-glass replacement dropped in -- an original will fit its well exactly and show matching wear. Estimate is at the top of the band before any of that is verified.
patience: Moderate. Tea caddies appear at every English-furniture sale; complete ones with the bowl are the exception.

analysis: An Iznik blue and white bowl at $600-800. The first of a four-lot Ottoman group (2431, 2434, 2436, 2438). Late Iznik and its Kutahya successors are genuinely 17th-century and satisfy the age criterion better than almost anything else in the sale, but they need to be told apart from the 19th-century revival ware -- Theodore Deck, late Kutahya and Turkish tourist production -- which copies the same designs on a clean white body with bright, stable colours.
problems: Condition is the whole question in this group. Iznik of this date is almost never found undamaged, and dishes far more often than bowls. Get the piece under a light and look for filled breaks and overpainted rim losses; restoration on Islamic pottery is often extensive and skilfully hidden. At $600-800 the estimate leaves no room for a restoration discount.
patience: Moderate to low. Genuine 17th-c. Iznik does not run regularly at a Maine regional house -- this four-lot consignment is the anomaly, not the pattern.

analysis: A Turkish Iznik dish, and this one the photograph does settle on period: the palette has degraded exactly the way late Iznik does -- the Armenian bole red has gone brown-black and sits proud of the surface, the greens have muddied, the cobalt has softened into the glaze -- and the body is a warm off-white rather than the bright clean white of 19th-century revival ware. A stylised rock-and-wave or saz-leaf rim band with a small green-and-yellow medallion at the centre. Genuinely 17th century, genuinely in the spirit of the age criterion.
problems: It is broken. The photograph shows long radiating cracks running from the centre out through the cavetto and into the rim on at least four axes -- this dish has been broken and reassembled, or is holding together on a stable but total network of breaks. There is heavy rim chipping and glaze loss around the edge. That is normal for the type and it is why the estimate is $600-800 rather than several thousand, but it caps what this can ever be worth and it is not a piece to bid up on the period alone.
patience: Moderate to low, but 2431/2436/2438 are three more chances in this same sale -- let them compete with each other.

analysis: The third Iznik dish, same estimate and presumably the same consignment as 2431 and 2434. Where four comparable lots run consecutively the room usually spends itself on the first one or two; the later lots in a block are where the value is. Assess all four in the room and bid the cheapest.
problems: Assume the same condition profile as 2434 -- breaks, rim loss and possible restoration -- until proved otherwise at preview. Same $600-800 estimate leaves no restoration discount.

analysis: Twenty-five Ottoman Turkish Iznik tiles in three boxes, catalogued as 'rescued from rubble' -- so architectural fragments from a demolished or damaged building, which is where nearly all loose Iznik tile on the market comes from. At $500-750 for twenty-five that is $20-30 a tile, and even fragmentary period Iznik tile runs $75-250 each. This is the best-value lot in the Ottoman group by some distance, on the arithmetic.
problems: 'Rescued from rubble' is honest cataloguing and also a warning: expect chips, mortar residue on the backs, cut edges and a proportion of pieces that are unusable. Twenty-five in three boxes cannot be assessed from two photographs -- open the boxes at preview and count what is whole. There is also a provenance question worth taking seriously on architectural fragments from the Ottoman world; check the consignment paperwork. Some 'Iznik' tile on the market is 19th-c. Kutahya revival at a tenth the value, and a mixed box is where that lands.
patience: Low. Boxed tile lots are irregular supply.

analysis: Two Safavid copper bowls at $1,000-1,200 -- above the budget band before the premium, and $1,320-1,584 all-in. Genuinely interesting material and genuinely old if right, but out of reach and outside every criterion except age.
problems: Safavid tinned-copper vessels with engraved calligraphic bands are among the most reproduced objects in the Persian decorative market; Isfahan has made them continuously for the tourist trade since the 19th century, and the fakes use the same forms, the same engraving and artificial patination. Establishing period needs a specialist. At this estimate there is no margin for being wrong.
patience: Moderate. Persian metalwork runs periodically; it is not scarce.

analysis: A framed Fischer & Mieg porcelain plaque with a hunting scene, $1,000-1,500. Fischer & Mieg of Pirkenhammer, Bohemia is a documented factory and painted porcelain plaques of this type are the good end of the Continental decorative market. But $1,000-1,500 hammer is $1,320-1,980 all-in, comfortably above the band.
problems: Above budget. Also: Bohemian factories sold blank plaques to outside decorators, so a factory mark on the reverse tells you who made the porcelain, not who painted it -- the painting quality is what matters and it needs to be seen. Hunting scenes are the most commonly painted and least sought subject in the genre.
patience: Moderate. Painted plaques run regularly; good ones are the minority.

analysis: Six Russian Imperial Porcelain Factory soup plates, Alexander II period. The reverse photograph settles it: a green underglaze crowned cypher mark of the Alexander II type with a date, which is the correct factory mark for 1855-1881. The faces carry a gilt-and-red crowned monogram. This is the best-documented ceramic lot in the sale -- the highest-status porcelain factory in Europe, a reign-dated mark, and genuine imperial service ware. It is also $1,000-1,500, which is $1,320-1,980 all-in and out of the band. If it stalls under $1,000 in the room it becomes interesting; do not plan on it.
problems: Above budget. There is a stained or restored area on the foot ring of the plate photographed from beneath -- check all six. The front cypher is hard to read at photograph resolution and does not obviously match an Alexander II monogram; the backstamp is the authority, but reconcile the two at preview before paying imperial money. IPF marks are forged, though usually on higher-value pieces than soup plates.
patience: Low. Reign-marked Imperial Porcelain does not come through Maine often.

spread: The range is an attribution question, not a valuation. A genuine Deng Bishan plaque and a Jingdezhen plaque signed in his name are the same object to a photograph and an order of magnitude apart in value. No margin is shown because averaging that spread would be inventing a number.
analysis: A Chinese porcelain carp plaque attributed to Deng Bishan (1874-1930). Deng Bishan was a real and significant Jingdezhen porcelain painter of the Republic period, in the circle around the Eight Friends of Zhushan, and a genuine signed plaque by him is a five-figure object. This is estimated $300-400. That gap is the whole story: the house has written 'attributed to' and then priced it as a decorative plaque, which is the house telling you what it actually thinks. Per the standing principle on estimates an order of magnitude below a genuine work, believe the estimate, not the name.
problems: Deng Bishan is among the most forged of the Republic-period painters; signed carp plaques in his manner are produced in quantity in Jingdezhen today and sold openly. Establishing a real one needs a specialist reading of the calligraphy, the seal, the enamel quality and the frame. My market range spans more than tenfold, which is unresolved attribution rather than value -- that is why no margin is shown. If you like the picture, buy it as an anonymous Republic-style plaque at $200-300 and treat any upside as a lottery ticket.
patience: High as a decorative plaque; low as a real Deng Bishan, but you will not get one of those at Thomaston.

analysis: 'Chinese Longquan STYLE celadon bowl', $500-750 -- the highest estimate in the Day 1 Chinese block. 'Style' is the cataloguer declining to commit to a period, and on Longquan that decision is doing a lot of work: real Song and Yuan Longquan is a museum market, and 'Longquan style' means a 20th-century copy of it. Priced as though the room might not read the word.
problems: Highest estimate in the block on the weakest attribution language in the block. No date offered anywhere in the title.

analysis: 'Chinese Yue ware STYLE celadon wine ewer', $200-300. Same construction as 1371 -- a famous early ware name defused by the word 'style'. Yue ware proper is Tang and earlier. This is a modern studio or export copy.
problems: 'Style' with no date. Estimate is above what unattributed decorative celadon makes.

analysis: 'Chinese Ming Dynasty STYLE blue and white meiping vase', $200-300. The title says Ming in order to say not-Ming. First lot of the large Day 1 Chinese decorative block (1341-1445), a consignment of roughly thirty vases and bowls almost all estimated $300-400 -- that uniformity is the tell that the house lotted a decorator's collection at a flat rate rather than valuing pieces individually.
problems: 'Style', no date, no mark discussed. The whole block should be treated as one decision.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain low vase', $300-400 -- a title with no date, no dynasty, no glaze named and no mark. Part of the flat-rate Day 1 Chinese block. When a cataloguer cannot find anything to say about a piece beyond its country and its shape, the piece is decorative.
problems: No information of any kind in the title. Estimate is the block's default number, not a valuation.

analysis: 'Chinese crackle glaze vase', $300-400. Crackle-glaze Chinese vases are the single most-produced decorative export ceramic of the last century. No date, no mark. Part of the Day 1 block.
problems: Nothing dates it. The estimate is the block default.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain vase', $300-400. The most contentless title in the block -- three words, no date, no form, no glaze. Decorative.
problems: No information. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese rectangular bottle vase', $300-400. Form named, nothing else. Part of the Day 1 flat-rate block.
problems: No date, no mark, no glaze. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese yellow ground bulbous vase', $300-400. Yellow-ground porcelain was an imperial prerogative in the Qing, which is exactly why it is the most copied ground colour in modern decorative export ware. No date, no mark discussed.
problems: Imperial-associated colour with no imperial attribution is a decorative copy. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain baluster vase', $300-400 -- one of four identically titled baluster vases in the block (1358, 1361, 1377 and, with a glaze named, 1360). Four of the same thing at the same number confirms the flat-rate lotting.
problems: No date, no mark. Competing directly with three near-identical lots in the same session.
patience: Very high -- there are three more in this sale.

analysis: 'Chinese mustard glazed baluster vase', $300-400. A glaze colour is the only added information over its three sibling lots. Decorative.
problems: No date, no mark. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain baluster vase', $300-400 -- word for word the same title as 1358 and 1377, three lots apart. Decorative.
problems: No date, no mark, no distinguishing feature from its siblings.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain globular vase', $300-400. One of three globular vases in the block (1363, 1367, 1375). Decorative, undated, unmarked.
problems: Block default estimate with no supporting information.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain pear shaped vase', $300-400. Form only. Decorative.
problems: No date, no mark. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese globular porcelain vase', $300-400 -- the same object as 1363 with the adjectives reordered. Decorative.
problems: No date, no mark.

analysis: Chinese 'Nine Peaches' porcelain charger, $300-400. Nine peaches is a famous Qing imperial famille rose design, endlessly reproduced in Republic-period and modern export ware. A genuine 18th-century example does not appear in a $300-400 slot in a Maine general sale.
problems: Famous design, no date, no mark, block-default estimate. The best-known decoration in the block and therefore the most copied.

analysis: 'Chinese footed censer', $300-400. No material named, no date, no mark. Censers are a heavily reproduced form -- bronze and porcelain alike -- because the archaic shapes are easy to copy and hard to date.
problems: The title does not even commit to what it is made of. Block default estimate.

analysis: Chinese globular dragon and phoenix vase, $300-400. Dragon-and-phoenix is the standard export decorative pairing. Third globular vase in the block.
problems: No date, no mark. Block default estimate.

analysis: 'Chinese porcelain baluster vase', $300-400 -- third lot with this exact title. Decorative.
problems: No date, no mark, indistinguishable from 1358 and 1361 on the catalogue alone.

analysis: Three-piece Chinese famille rose porcelain jar on stand, $300-400. Jar, cover and carved stand. Famille rose export jars on hardwood stands are the standard decorator import of the last seventy years.
problems: No date, no mark. A fitted stand adds display value and no age evidence.

analysis: A pair of Chinese famille rose figural porcelain vase lamps, $200-300. Mounted as lamps, which means drilled, wired and fitted -- and the mounting is nearly always mid-20th-century American decorator work on mid-20th-century Chinese vases. Not antique in any reading.
problems: Drilled bases destroy whatever collector value the porcelain had. Wiring on lamps of this age is a safety question. No date.
patience: Very high. There are four more Chinese vase-lamp lots in this sale alone (2481, 2487, 2497).

analysis: A pair of Chinese blue and white barbed rim chargers, $300-500. Barbed-rim chargers copy Ming and Kangxi originals and are made continuously for the decorative trade. Nothing in the title dates them.
problems: No date, no mark, no reign-mark discussion. Pairs of matching chargers surviving from any real age is itself unlikely.

analysis: A cased set of eighteen Chinese porcelain 'warriors' vases, $300-400 -- and there are three identical lots, 1394, 1396 and 1398, all the same description and all the same estimate. Three identical cased sets of eighteen is not a collection; it is unsold stock. This is modern Jingdezhen tourist and gift ware, made in presentation cases for exactly this purpose.
problems: Three identical lots in one session competing against each other. Fitted presentation cases are a retail signal, not an age signal. Estimate is several times what these make.
patience: Very high -- there are two more in this sale.

analysis: Second of the three identical cased sets of eighteen 'warriors' vases. See 1394.
problems: Identical to 1394 and 1398 in the same session.

analysis: Third of the three identical cased sets of eighteen 'warriors' vases. See 1394.
problems: Identical to 1394 and 1396 in the same session.

analysis: A ten-piece Chinese porcelain collection, $300-500. The word 'collection' with no piece named, no date and no maker is a box lot. Ten unspecified pieces at $30-50 each.
problems: Unknowable from the catalogue. If bidding at all, view it in person and value the best single piece, not the count.

analysis: A pair of Chinese Swatow porcelain low bowls, $300-400. Real Swatow ware is late Ming export stoneware and a genuine 16th-17th-century pair would not sit in a $300-400 slot. The name is being used descriptively for the style.
problems: A specific historic ware name with no date attached. Block default estimate.

analysis: An Annamese blue and white charger, $200-300. Annamese (Vietnamese) blue and white of the 15th-16th century is a real and collected category, largely known from the Hoi An shipwreck cargo -- and shipwreck-recovery pieces have flooded the market since the 1990s, so even genuine ones are cheap. No date given here.
problems: No date, no provenance, no mention of shipwreck recovery. Vietnamese wares are also widely reproduced for the tourist trade.

analysis: 'Chinese blue and white pottery bowl', $300-400. Pottery rather than porcelain, no date, no mark. Last of the Day 1 Chinese block.
problems: No information. Block default estimate.

analysis: A 'Mexican Aztec red clay tripod vase', $400-600. Genuine pre-Columbian Aztec ceramics are subject to Mexican patrimony law and US import restriction and do not appear unremarked in a general sale; what does appear in quantity is 20th-century Mexican tourist replica ware, which is what this almost certainly is.
problems: If it were genuinely pre-Columbian, the legal and provenance questions would make it unbuyable without documentation. If it is a replica, $400-600 is roughly five times the market. Either way the answer is no.

analysis: A Chinese hexagonal porcelain garden seat, $600-800 -- one of three garden-stool lots on Day 2 (2182, 2188, 2211). This is the only one with no date at all in the title, while the other two are catalogued 'late Qing' and '19th century'. That asymmetry is informative: when the same cataloguer dates two of three, the undated one is the one they could not date.
problems: No date, and the estimate matches the dated examples. Garden seats are large, heavy, and made continuously for the export market. Above the comfortable band at $792-1,056 all-in.

analysis: A Chinese blue and white porcelain garden stool, catalogued late Qing -- so a stated pre-1912 date the house can be held to, which is more than most of the Chinese material here offers. $600-800 estimate is $792-1,056 all-in, at or above the top of the band, for a large decorative object.
problems: Above the band. Garden stools are heavy, awkward and vulnerable -- check the whole circumference for restored breaks at the pierced medallions, which is where they always go. The late Qing dating is catalogued but not evidenced.
patience: High. Garden stools run regularly and prices have been falling with the wider Chinese decorative market.

analysis: A Chinese blue-glazed porcelain garden stool, catalogued 19th century. Third of the Day 2 garden-stool group at the same $600-800. Monochrome blue is the plainer and less commercial of the two glaze choices in this group.
problems: Above the band at $792-1,056 all-in. Same structural fragility as 2188. A single-colour glaze shows every chip and firing flaw.

analysis: A Chinese blue and white crackle-glazed bowl, $400-600. Undated, in a Day 2 Chinese group (2465-2499) where the cataloguer does date several neighbouring lots -- so the absence of a date here is a choice.
problems: No date, no mark. Estimate is well above the market for undated decorative crackle ware.

analysis: A pair of Chinese famille rose figural vases, catalogued Republic period. The date is stated and it is post-1926 for most of its range, so this fails the age criterion outright. Republic-period famille rose is decorative export ware unless it carries a documented painter's name -- and this does not.
problems: Post-1926 by the house's own dating. $400-600 for decorative Republic vases is above the market.

analysis: A Chinese clair-de-lune glazed phoenix-tail vase, catalogued 19th century, $500-700. Clair-de-lune is a refined Qing monochrome and the phoenix-tail form is a good one; catalogued to the century, so the age criterion is met on a claim rather than a guess. But $660-924 all-in for a decorative monochrome vase with no mark discussed is at the top of the band with nothing distinguishing it.
problems: Monochrome glazes hide nothing -- every chip, crack and glaze flaw is visible, so condition matters more here than on decorated wares. No reign mark mentioned. The Chinese decorative market has fallen substantially since 2015 and monochromes have fallen with it.

analysis: A Chinese robin's-egg glazed porcelain meiping vase, $400-500. Robin's-egg (lujun) is a Qing imperial glaze and is copied constantly. Undated in a group where the cataloguer dates other lots.
problems: No date, no mark. Estimate assumes an age nobody has claimed.

analysis: A Chinese Longquan celadon glazed charger, $800-1,200 -- the highest-estimated Chinese ceramic in the sale and, tellingly, one with no date attached. Compare 1371, where the cataloguer wrote 'Longquan STYLE' for a $500-750 bowl. Dropping the qualifier here while raising the estimate, without adding a date, is the estimate carrying an implication the words will not.
problems: Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in. No date, no provenance, no discussion of the body or foot -- which is where a real Longquan piece is authenticated. This is the lot in the Chinese material most likely to catch someone out.

analysis: A Chinese yellow-glazed moulded dragon bowl, $300-400. Yellow ground plus dragon is the imperial combination and therefore the most reproduced. No date, no reign mark discussed.
problems: Imperial iconography with no imperial attribution and no date. If there is an apocryphal reign mark on the base -- which there almost certainly is -- it is decoration, not evidence.

analysis: A Chinese powder-blue ground famille verte porcelain jar mounted as a lamp, $600-800. One of three vase-lamp lots on Day 2 (2481, 2487, 2497) plus 1381 on Day 1. Mounting means drilling and fitting, which is decorator work of the mid-20th century regardless of the jar's age.
problems: Drilled. Above the band at $792-1,056 all-in. Old wiring. No date on the porcelain.
patience: Very high -- there are three more lamp conversions in this sale.

analysis: A Chinese blue-ground porcelain jar lamp, $500-700. See 2481 -- same conversion, plainer decoration, slightly lower estimate.
problems: Drilled and wired. No date. Estimate well above the decorator-lamp market.

analysis: Three Chinese blue and white porcelain vase lamps, $300-500. The third lamp lot on Day 2 and the only one grouped in threes -- three lamps at $100-165 each is the most honest pricing in the group.
problems: All three drilled and wired. No date on any. Nothing here fits a criterion.

analysis: A pair of Chinese lidded urns, $400-600. No date, no glaze named, no decoration described, no mark. Even by the standards of this consignment the title is empty.
problems: Nothing to assess. Lids on Chinese urns are frequently replacements or associated; check that both match their bodies. Estimate is a default.

analysis: A Chinese celadon jade dragon bangle, catalogued late Qing, $500-700. Not a ceramic at all -- it lands here on the word 'celadon' -- but it is worth treating with the jade discipline applied elsewhere in this analysis. Catalogued to the late Qing, so the age criterion is met on a claim.
problems: 'Celadon jade' should mean nephrite, but the term is used loosely and the same descriptions cover serpentine, bowenite and dyed quartzite. Carved dragon bangles are made in enormous quantity in modern China. Distinguishing nephrite needs specific gravity and a refractometer, not a photograph -- this is a preview or gemmologist question and there is no melt-style floor to fall back on. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band with the material itself unverified.
patience: High. Jade bangles run constantly and almost all of them raise this same question.

analysis: A Chinese 'Sanxing' porcelain plaque, catalogued 19th century, $500-700. Sanxing are the three star gods -- Fu, Lu and Shou -- an extremely common auspicious subject. Catalogued to the century, so the date is a claim rather than a guess, which is more than most of this group offers. But $660-924 all-in for a decorative enamelled plaque of a standard subject is the top of the band.
problems: Above the comfortable band, common subject, no painter named. Porcelain plaques crack and the frame usually hides the edges; check the reverse.

analysis: A Chinese Canton enamel on copper plate, $200-400. Canton enamel is a real 18th-19th-century export ware, but the form has been made continuously ever since and the modern versions are visually close. No date offered.
problems: No date, no mark. Canton enamel chips and flakes from the copper at the rim; check the edge. Estimate is above the undated market.

analysis: Diana Kan (China, 1926-2010), $600-800 -- a painting, not a ceramic; it falls here only because it closes the Day 2 Chinese consignment. Kan was a Chinese-American painter in the Lingnan-influenced splashed-ink manner, a documented and mildly collected name. Born 1926, so the work is necessarily post-1926 and cannot meet the age criterion.
problems: Above the comfortable band at $792-1,056 all-in. No medium, no title, no date given -- ink-and-colour on paper and later prints or reproductions after her work both circulate. Wrong subject matter for this collection.
patience: High. Kan's work turns up regularly in American regional sales.

analysis: 'Pair of gargantuan Romanesque yellow garden urns', $1,000-1,500, and no lot number in the catalogue data -- one of two unnumbered lots in the sale. 'Romanesque' here is a shape description, not a date. Above the band, enormous, and undated.
problems: Above budget at $1,320-1,980 all-in. No lot number means no reliable way to bid online. 'Gargantuan' garden ware is a shipping and siting problem as much as a purchase. Cast or moulded garden urns of this type are made new continuously.
